extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, policymakers and transport/rail safety professionals interested in the Lac-Mégantic disaster and regulatory responses
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of regulatory, safety, and legal standards and actions taken after the Lac-Mégantic oil-by-rail disaster, including emergency directives, inspection programs, tank-car design changes, and litigation/compensation rules. Focuses on Canada and the United States responses and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport Canada emergency directive (23 July 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directive requiring at least two persons operate trains carrying tank cars of dangerous materials; prohibiting dangerous material trains left on the mainline unattended; requiring locomotive cabs on unattended trains be locked and reverser handles removed to prevent the train being put into gear; imposing requirements for setting hand brakes on trains unattended for more than an hour; and requiring both the automatic brake (train brake) and independent brake (locomotive brake) be applied at their maximum force for trains unattended for an hour or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ministerial emergency directive remains in effect for six months, although it can be renewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRA emergency orders (2 August 2013) — notification and train securement
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders requiring U.S. railroad operating companies to develop and submit plans to the FRA to notify the agency when trains carrying hazardous materials will be left unattended, and to implement processes to secure the trains in their positions and to ensure locomotive doors are locked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before leaving a train unattended, railroad crews needed to notify dispatchers of the number of hand brakes being applied on the train along with the number of cars, the train length, the grade of the track on which the train is parked and the current weather conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper identification and testing of crude oil composition and flash point on shipping manifests
rubrics_metrics.description: Shippers were not properly identifying the chemical composition and flash point of flammable cargo on shipping manifests; blended crude from multiple wells was not being tested before loading, preventing correct classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FRA indicated it is critical that shippers determine the proper classification of the crude oil because a tanker with a higher safety classification (not the standard DOT-111A) is required for corrosive or explosive materials; accurate content information is needed for first responders and emergency services during a disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: TSB recommendation — replace older DOT-111/CTC-111A tank cars
rubrics_metrics.description: Transportation Safety Board recommended that DOT-111 / CTC-111A oil-by-rail cars built before October 2011 be replaced with the newer, reinforced design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSB also recommended carriers perform route planning and analysis and advocated mandated emergency response plans. (TSB set no clear deadlines; some operators like Irving Oil announced voluntary replacement schedules.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrier route planning and mandated emergency response plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation and later regulatory moves that carriers perform route planning and analysis and that emergency response plans be mandated for oil-by-rail shipments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSB advocated mandated emergency response plans; subsequent government actions (see Canadian regulations) moved to require emergency response planning for oil shipments by rail.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. FRA reclassification and pre-shipment testing of crude oil (Feb 2014)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Railroad Administration placed crude oil under the most protective two sets of hazardous materials shipping requirements and issued an order requiring tests of crude oil before shipment by rail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This elevates the protective shipping classification applied to crude and requires empirical testing to determine classification before transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canadian government regulation (April 2014) — phaseout/retrofit and emergency response mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Canadian government required a phaseout or retrofit of older DOT-111 oil-by-rail cars on a three-year deadline and mandated emergency response plans for all oil shipments by rail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory/regulatory mandate (three-year timeline) as opposed to TSB's recommendations which lacked specific deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspections and data collection ('Bakken blitz' and API data request)
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration launched targeted inspections of North Dakota oil trains ('Bakken blitz') citing concerns about improper identification of chemical composition and flash point; FRA requested American Petroleum Institute members provide data on crude content and loading practices and proposed to test themselves if data were not provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory oversight actions intended to gather industry data and verify safe loading and classification practices; failure to cooperate could prompt regulator testing and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securement of unattended locomotives and trains — TSB advisory letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Transportation Safety Board of Canada issued safety advisory letters (e.g., RAIL SAFETY ADVISORY LETTER – 08/13 and 09/13) concerning the securement of unattended locomotives and equipment and trains left unattended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory letters describe securement practices and encourage regulatory/industry action to ensure unattended equipment is properly secured to prevent runaway incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tank corrosion and overloading risk mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification that chemicals used in fracking (e.g., hydrochloric acid) can corrode tanks, covers, valves and fittings, and that unit trains often bypass weigh-in-motion scales in classification yards leading to overloaded tank cars and greater leakage risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation implies testing for corrosive components, ensuring tanks and fittings are compatible, performing weight checks (weigh-in-motion) to avoid overloading, and recognizing higher leak/incident rates when these controls are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal remedies and jurisdictional differences in damage caps
rubrics_metrics.description: Canadian courts can award plaintiffs a maximum of $326,000 as compensation for non-economic damages like emotional distress; in the U.S. (example: Illinois), there may be no limit on non-economic damage awards, and plaintiffs sought varying amounts (e.g., over $50 million in one Chicago case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in caps and remedies across jurisdictions affect litigation strategy, settlement expectations, and timelines; bankruptcy filings (MMA Chapter 11 and CCAA) also influence progress and possible settlement structures.
